title: Solomon, Jeroboam, and Naboth’s Vineyard
english: …by way of examples, taking up our own members; only in this way do we rise, and barely, to faint thoughts about God.

“And the queen of Sheba,” and so on (1 Kings 10:1). (Cyril, from his Commentary on Luke.) A foreign woman, though great distances kept her away, overcame her reluctance, not to gather riches but to hear the wisdom of Solomon, who spoke in parables and riddles and sketched both the beauties and the faults of human character.

“Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh, the idol of Moab” (1 Kings 11:7). What could be more grievous than such monstrous offenses: to assign to herds of demons the dignity of honor and love that belongs to the one God, who is God by nature; or rather, to fashion them out of stones and wood, and to build temples for them?

“And the Lord was angry with Solomon,” and so on (1 Kings 11:9). And what, then, had been commanded to him and to all men under the Law? That they should not marry foreigners. For he said: “You shall not give your daughter to his son, and you shall not take his daughter for your son. For he will turn your son away from me, and he will go and serve other gods” (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). Forgetting this command, then, he joined himself to the daughters of foreigners. “Since, then,” he says, “you have counted as nothing the command that was given, and have slipped into apostasy and served the gods of foreigners; and since, though you knew that creation is my servant, you have assigned to it the honor and glory that are mine and that befit me alone, I too will tear your kingdom apart and give it to your servant (1 Kings 11:11), so that you may learn what you have done from what has happened to you.”

For Solomon, very wise though he was, was overcome by his desires for women, and all but tore apart the kingdom of God, so far as his efforts could reach, by attaching to idols the honor and glory that befit God alone. For this very reason God threatened, and with good cause, to tear his kingdom apart, grieving him in equal measure, as it is written in the prophet Ezekiel: “As you have done, so it shall be to you; your recompense shall be repaid upon your head” (Obadiah 1:15; compare Ezekiel 16:59).

“And the king took counsel, and went, and made two calves” (1 Kings 12:28). Jeroboam became the author of ruin for the people of Israel, displaying their choice of the kingship of men instead, and their turning away from being ruled by God through prophets. For: “See, Jeroboam has provoked me, the Master, by devising new calves and investing them with my own dignity.” And again: At the start Jeroboam devised the calves and ordered the customary rites to be performed before them, the wretch, attaching to his own inventions the glory that befits God, so that he himself might hold the kingdom securely; and so he robs God, as it were, of what is his own.

“And Naboth had a vineyard” (1 Kings 21:1). Isaiah teaches us to understand the vineyard as Israel (Isaiah 5:7). But its leaders, of whom Ahab bears the type, longed to have it; yet they could not persuade him to betray to them his father’s choice vineyard, so that they might turn it into a vegetable garden, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men (Matthew 15:9), and giving…

title: Naboth as Christ, and Prompt Obedience to God
english: …it a muddy drink that overthrows (Habakkuk 2:15). Then what did Jezebel, hateful to God, do, that is, the synagogue of the Jews, joining in the grief of its leaders? By deceit she pursues the righteous Naboth, that is, the One who is to come. For Emmanuel was put to death on false charges.

“The God of Israel is a God of mountains” (1 Kings 20:23). For they supposed that the Israelites had won because God could save only on the mountains, or perhaps on the hills as well. “So we were defeated,” it says, “because the God of Israel is a God of mountains; but if we should meet in battle on bare plains, we shall surely prevail, since the God of Israel is powerless in the valleys.” These are the faults of pagan madness, the dreadful unbridled tongue of those who do not know the true God, who is God by nature. So God, who is mighty in all things, was angry with the foreigners, and with very good reason, because when they defeated Israel, as I said, they credited their thank offerings to their own gods, and in their folly supposed that they had prevailed over God himself.

“And he found another man and said, ‘Strike me’” (1 Kings 20:37). Do you hear how the man who refused to strike the prophet was miserably killed when he fell in with a fierce beast? And yet how could it not be true to say that it was the fruit of reverence not to dare to strike down a holy man and a prophet? But since it was at the word of the Lord, disobedience became a charge hard to escape (1 Kings 20:35-36). So hard to escape is the charge of doing anything against what seems good to God, or of not doing without delay what he commands. It is necessary, then, that whatever pleases God be carried out by us without hesitation or delay. To do anything other than this, or even to choose to think otherwise, brings the charge of arrogance; for such people have all but resolved to rebuke God, as though he had sometimes not counseled rightly.
Book Four.

“And now you have taken the silver,” and so on (2 Kings 5:26). Christ too says this in the holy Gospels: “Carry no purse, no bag, no sandals; and greet no one on the road” (Luke 10:4). For one must go to the work with a straight course, and not even return a blessing to one who blesses. For turning aside to others is a loss to zeal, and so is spending idly, on things that are not necessary, the time that belongs to preaching; nor should one grant friendships the favor of useless delay.

“And they took possession of Samaria” (2 Kings 17:24). These, then, who took the land of the Samaritans as their lot and settled there, in time, it seems, became fathers of children; and they inclined toward the customs of the Jews, terrified by the attacks of the lions (2 Kings 17:25-26). From them came Sarasar and Arbeseser, who was also called king because at that time he led those who had been resettled in Samaria from the land of the Persians.

“Hezekiah the son of Ahaz, king of Judah, began to reign” (2 Kings 18:1). He had advanced so far in glory and in strength alike as to subdue the nations living around Judea, and indeed to impose heavy tribute on them. And a little further on: Then he suffered something human. For through excessive luxury, and overcome by the eminence of his fame, he became in a way proud; and, gripped by the disease of arrogance, he rose up against the divine law itself. For he thought…

title: The Assyrian Boast and Jerusalem’s Deliverance
english: …that he ought to crown himself with the honors of the divine priesthood as well. For he attempted to push his way into the divine temple, to burn incense to God by his own hand, and to perform the customary rites as the Law prescribes. For this reason he was struck with leprosy at once and was held in the deepest dishonor; for under the Law one gripped by the disease of leprosy is unclean.

“Where is the god of Hamath?” and so on; “Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand?” (2 Kings 18:34). For the barbarian, whose tongue matched his pride, perhaps supposed that the Master of earth and heaven, the Maker and Lord of all things, was just like one of the falsely named gods. Indeed it is the habit of those who do not know God sometimes to mock the hope of the saints, and to dare to say that they would not be delivered by God. Yet he was not unaware that human hands had made the falsely named gods, while the One who is God by nature and in truth was made by no one, but rather himself brought into being things that once did not exist. Samaria, then, was captured because God withheld his help. And, as I said before, even if none of the gods spoken of among the Greeks saved its own land, that counts for nothing against God, who truly and by nature exists and is great. For those gods have received from human craft only this much, that they can at least be seen; but he rules over all things, being the Lord of hosts.

“He tore his garments” (2 Kings 19:1). Do you see how, disregarding his own affairs, he grieves for God’s sake and seeks vengeance? “He tore his garments,” it says, “and covered himself with sackcloth, and went into the house of the Lord” (2 Kings 19:1). And what was the reason for tearing his clothes? It was the custom of the Jews to do this at blasphemies against God; and the Gospels record that Caiaphas did the same (Matthew 26:65).

“I cut down the height of its cedar” (2 Kings 19:23). Its: whose? Lebanon’s, that is, Judea’s. By the height of the cedar he means their kingdom. For the glories of Hezekiah’s kingdom were about to be raised on high.

“And I will put my hooks in your nostrils,” he says, “and a bridle in your lips” (2 Kings 19:28). So that he would not dare to utter such things. Yet even if he did not share the fate of the multitude, for the reason already stated, the same reason for which Pharaoh too was kept as an onlooker while the rest of the Egyptians were punished, still he found his own sons to be his murderers when he had come back to his own land (2 Kings 19:37).

“And I will shield this city for my own sake” (2 Kings 19:34). For this befits the One who is God. Therefore: “I will do these things for my own sake,” and not because those who are helped are worthy.

“And the angel of the Lord went out and struck down in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and eighty-five thousand” (2 Kings 19:35). So the war is ended, and the threats flee along with the dangers; and so from then on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, rejoicing greatly at the help that came from God, could say: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me” (Psalm 30:11). See how things are reversed; consider carefully what he says: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me.” Great was the mourning because of the multitude of those making war; great has the joy become because of the multitude of those who have fallen.
